sections.text: धृतराष्ट्र उवाच। धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः। मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय
Dhritarashtra said: O Sanjaya, assembled on the holy field of Kurukshetra, eager to fight, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do?
सञ्जय उवाच। दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा। आचार्यमुपसङ्गम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्
Sanjaya replied: Having seen the Pandava army arranged in battle formation, King Duryodhana approached his teacher Drona and spoke.
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम्। व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता
O Teacher, look at this great army of Pandus sons, arranged by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.

Think about this for a moment: the Bhagavad Gita doesnt begin with Krishna. It doesnt begin with Arjuna. It begins with a blind man asking a question from his palace, miles away from the battlefield.
Dhritarashtra couldnt see. But his blindness wasnt just physical, and thats precisely the point.
The day before this war, the sage Vyasa came to Dhritarashtra and offered him something extraordinary. I can give you divine sight, Vyasa said. You can witness everything that happens on this battlefield.
Dhritarashtras response? No, thank you. Im comfortable as I am. But if youre offering, give it to Sanjaya instead.
Im comfortable in my blindness.
How many times have we said the same thing, in different words? We dont want to see whats really happening in our marriage. We dont want to acknowledge what that habit is doing to us. Wed rather not look too closely at how were living our lives. Chosen blindness feels easier than facing difficult truths.
The Gita begins here because this is where most of us begin, not wanting to see.
Now look at the first words Dhritarashtra speaks: Dharmakshetre Kurukshetre, at the field of Dharma, at Kurukshetra.
He calls it Dharmakshetra. The field of righteousness. He knows. Somewhere deep down, Dhritarashtra knows exactly which side represents Dharma in this war. Hes not confused about right and wrong. He simply cant bring himself to act on what he knows.
This is one of the Gitas earliest teachings, tucked into its very first line: knowing whats right is not the same as doing whats right. Dhritarashtra knew. He just couldnt act.
Theres something else hidden in this verse, a single word that reveals everything about why this war is happening. The word is Māmakāḥ, mine.
What did my sons and Pandus sons do?
But wait. Werent they all grandsons of the same man? Werent the Pandavas also descendants of Kuru? Why arent they all simply Kauravas?
Because Dhritarashtra couldnt see them that way. My children versus their children. My family versus those people. This is how he saw the world. This is how the world always divides itself before it goes to war.
We do this too, dont we? My team versus their team. My community versus outsiders. We draw these lines constantly, and then we wonder why theres so much conflict. The Gita is pointing at something fundamental here: this mine versus yours thinking is the seed from which all conflict grows.
In verse 2, the scene shifts to the battlefield. Sanjaya begins his narration, and immediately we see something curious: Duryodhana, the mighty king with the larger army, is nervous.
He had eleven akshauhinis, massive military divisions. The Pandavas had only seven. By any calculation, he should win. Yet look at what he does: he rushes to his teacher Drona, not to the commander Bhishma, and starts anxiously pointing out the enemys strengths.
Why would someone with such an advantage feel so unsettled?
Because numbers arent everything. Duryodhana knew, in some part of himself, that he was on the wrong side of this fight. He had stolen a kingdom. He had tried to kill his cousins. He had humiliated Draupadi in open court. All the military might in the world couldnt quiet that knowledge.
This is something worth sitting with: when youre doing the right thing, you can face challenges with a certain peace. When youre not, no amount of external advantage makes you feel secure. Duryodhana had everything going for him, except the one thing that would have given him real confidence.
And then comes verse 3, where Duryodhana speaks to Drona. On the surface, hes just pointing out the Pandava formation. But listen to his words more carefully: Look at this army, arranged by the son of Drupada, your wise disciple.
Theres an accusation buried in that phrase. Your disciple. The one you taught. Duryodhana is essentially saying: This is your fault, teacher. You trained them. You gave them the skills theyre now using against us.
This is how it works when were not willing to own our choices. We blame the teacher, the parents, the circumstances, the system, anyone but ourselves. Duryodhana never once stopped to ask: How did my own actions lead us here? Instead, he looked for someone else to hold responsible.
Theres a deeper teaching embedded in the structure of these opening verses that often gets overlooked. Notice how Vyasa, the author, chose to begin the text. He could have started with Krishnas teaching. He could have opened with some grand philosophical statement about the nature of reality. Instead, he begins with a question born from anxiety.
Dhritarashtra asks: Kim akurvata, what did they do? Hes desperate to know. He cant bear the uncertainty. And this desperation reveals something crucial about the nature of attachment.
When we are deeply attached to an outcome, uncertainty becomes unbearable. We need to know. We check our phones constantly. We ask the same questions over and over. We cannot rest until we have information that confirms or denies our hopes and fears.
Dhritarashtra is not simply curious about the battle. He is terrified. His whole sense of security, the kingdom he helped his son steal, the dynasty he hoped to establish, depends on the outcome of this war. No wonder hes asking questions before a single arrow has been fired.
The Gita begins this way to show us something about ourselves. How much of our mental activity is driven by this same anxious need to know? How much of our day is spent checking, confirming, seeking reassurance?
Kurukshetra was not just any battlefield, it was considered sacred ground. The name literally means field of the Kurus, the ancestral dynasty. But it was also called Dharmakshetra because it was a place where great sages had performed austerities and spiritual practices for generations.
Theres a profound symbolism here. The battle for dharma, for right living, doesnt happen in some pristine spiritual environment away from the mess of life. It happens right here, on the same ground where our ancestors walked, where our family dramas play out, where the stakes are highest and the relationships most complicated.
You dont get to choose a convenient time and place for your spiritual growth. The battlefield finds you. It might be your workplace, your marriage, your relationship with your aging parents, your own health crisis. The question is never how do I avoid the battle? The question is how do I face it with clarity?
Consider also the role of Sanjaya in these verses. Hes the narrator, the one with divine sight, granted by Vyasa. Throughout the Gita, Sanjaya reports whats happening on the battlefield to the blind king.
Sanjaya represents something important: the possibility of true seeing. Unlike Dhritarashtra, who chose blindness, Sanjaya accepted the gift of vision. He can see the truth, and he reports it faithfully, even when that truth is painful to hear.
Every one of us has access to our own inner Sanjaya, that part of us that knows the truth, that sees clearly, that isnt fooled by our rationalizations. The question is: do we listen to it? Or do we, like Dhritarashtra, prefer to remain comfortable in our blindness?
The Gita is, in one sense, an invitation to become our own Sanjaya, to develop the capacity to see our lives clearly, to witness our own dramas with some degree of objectivity, to tell ourselves the truth even when its inconvenient.
One more thing worth noting about these opening verses: the emotional tone. Theres urgency here. Theres anxiety. Theres blame. Theres defensiveness. The battlefield hasnt even begun, and already we see the full range of human reactivity on display.
This is intentional. The Gita doesnt pretend that we come to spiritual teaching from a place of calm readiness. We come to it desperate, confused, looking for someone to blame, terrified of what might happen. We come to it exactly as Arjuna will come to it in the verses ahead, overwhelmed and unable to function.
And thats okay. Thats the starting point. The Gita meets us where we are.
Finally, lets consider the setting of these opening verses from a practical perspective. Here is Duryodhana, about to fight the most important battle of his life, and instead of focusing on strategy or inspiring his troops, hes complaining to his teacher about the enemys strengths.
This is what anxiety does to us. It makes us focus on threats rather than possibilities. It makes us rehearse worst-case scenarios. It makes us seek validation for our fears rather than courage for our actions.
Duryodhana had assembled the greatest army the world had ever seen. He had legendary warriors on his side, Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Ashwatthama. He had every material advantage. And yet here he is, fixated on what the other side has, unable to appreciate his own resources.
We do this constantly. We have health, relationships, skills, opportunities, and we obsess over what we lack. We have support systems and capabilities, and we fixate on the obstacles. This is the Duryodhana mind at work, and it never leads anywhere good.
The antidote isnt positive thinking or denial of real challenges. The antidote is clarity, seeing what we actually have, what the situation actually requires, and acting from that clear seeing rather than from anxiety and complaint.
Thats the journey the Gita will take us on. But it starts here, with recognizing where we are: blind like Dhritarashtra, anxious like Duryodhana, looking for someone to blame. Only when we see this clearly can we begin to move beyond it.

These opening verses invite us to examine the Dhritarashtra within ourselves. Notice how he uses the word Mamakah, mine, creating an immediate division between my sons and Pandus sons, even though both groups are equally his nephews and part of the same Kuru dynasty. This week, observe where you draw similar lines in your own life. Where do you say my team versus their team, my community versus outsiders? The Gita suggests that this mine versus theirs thinking is the very seed from which all conflict grows.
Consider also the profound symbolism of Dhritarashtras chosen blindness. When Vyasa offered him divine sight to witness the battle, he refused, preferring the comfort of not seeing. Ask yourself: What truths am I choosing not to see in my own life? Is there a difficult conversation Im avoiding? A habit whose consequences I refuse to acknowledge? A relationship truth Id rather not face? Like Dhritarashtra, we often find comfort in blindness, but the Gita reminds us that this comfort comes at a terrible cost.
Finally, notice how Duryodhana, despite having the larger army (eleven akshauhinis versus seven), rushes nervously to his teacher Drona to point out the enemys strengths. This reveals a profound truth: when we know deep down that our cause is not righteous, no amount of external advantage brings real security. Reflect on areas of your life where you feel anxious despite having everything going for you. Could this anxiety be pointing to a misalignment between your actions and your deeper sense of what is right?
